children: The Securities and Exchange Commission accused Ernest Ossei Boateng and two New Jersey-based companies he controls of operating a $16 million Ponzi scheme, according to a civil complaint the regulator filed last week in a federal court in New York.

From January 2020 until at least March 2026, Boateng solicited money from more than 200 inexperienced investors, who were primarily Christians of Ghanaian heritage in New York and New Jersey, according to the SEC. The victims included members of a prayer group, the complaint says.
Michael Baldassare, an attorney representing Boateng, didn't respond to requests for comment.

Boateng told prospective investors that their investments would generate guaranteed annual returns on their money typically ranging from 25% to 100%, according to the SEC. He also said that he would pursue a low-risk investment strategy, according to the regulator.

Boateng allegedly misappropriated more than $5.8 million of investor funds for his personal expenses, including the purchase, renovation, and furnishing of his home, according to the regulator. The SEC also says that to the limited extent Boateng did invest the money, he did so in high-risk, speculative day trading and suffered more than $750,000 in trading losses. He also made approximately $6.6 million in Ponzi-like payments to earlier investors, the regulator says.

"We allege that the defendants' investors included retirees, taxi drivers, home healthcare providers, students, an ailing widow with young children, and at least two churches and one prayer group," says Thomas P. Smith, Jr., associate director of the SEC's New York Regional Office. "The defendants' sales pitch to victims included assuring them that their investments were safe and without risk-telling many their money was protected by so-called 'financial, investment insurance.'"

Boateng, 44, immigrated to the U.S. from Ghana in 2016, according to the SEC's complaint. He holds no professional or Finra licenses and has never been associated with a registered investment advisor or broker-dealer, the complaint says. In 2016, Boateng failed to pass two examinations that are required to become a registered representative in the brokerage industry, according to the regulator. His two companies, Intercontinental Wealth Network and I Wealth Network, were launched in July 2017 and in October 2020, respectively. Neither has any employees, according to the SEC.

To conceal the alleged scheme, Boateng provided fake account statements to investors, the SEC says. He affixed the logo of an SEC-registered brokerage firm on the statements to make them appear legitimate even though the brokerage firm had no role in their creation, according to the regulator, which didn't identify the firm in its legal complaint. When investors asked Boateng why they weren't receiving payments, he allegedly said that he couldn't because of purported administrative issues or that the SEC had "frozen" his accounts, which wasn't true, according to the regulator.
The SEC is asking the court for monetary penalties against Boateng and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains.
